newsitem.title: USA: EIA sees adequate distillate supplies for winter.
newsitem.headline: EIA sees adequate distillate supplies for winter.

text.p: U.S. heating oil and diesel supplies should be sufficient to meet demand this winter, despite concern about lean distillate stocks, but prices are likely to be higher, the Energy Information Administration said on Monday.
"I don't think you have a shortage situation, because a high price will always be able to find product somewhere," said EIA administrator Jay Hakes.
The outlook assumed that the upcoming winter would be normal, compared with the harsh winter earlier this year.

"As year-over-year distillate demand growth for the winter season is projected to be only 18,000 barrels per day, supplies from the three major sources -- domestic refinery production, net imports, and primary stocks -- should still be able to accommodate winter fuel requirements," EIA said in its winter fuels outlook.

EIA projected refinery output of distillate to average 3.25 million barrels per day in October through March, up 53,000 bpd from last year. Distillate production in the fourth quarter, the peak quarter, was expected to rise 75,000 bpd from a year ago to 3.36 million bpd.
Stocks of distillate at the beginning of winter were expected to be 19 million barrels below last year's level at about 113 million barrels.
To help fill inventories, net imports in the fourth quarter should average 81,000 bpd, compared with net exports of 39,000 bpd in the same quarter in 1995.
Stocks would likely be drawn down by 373,000 bpd in the first quarter of 1997, compared with 440,000 bpd in January through March this year, EIA said.

"Additional oil from the North Sea and other non-OPEC countries should provide enough oil for this winter's demand, although a colder than normal winter would greatly increase the likelihood of higher prices, given the little room for error in this year's market," EIA said.

If the weather is normal, home heating oil prices should be about 9 cents higher than last winter, averaging about $1.02 between October and March, largely because of the low inventories and higher crude prices, EIA said.
Imported crude prices are projected at $20.18 a barrel in the first half of winter and $19.17 in the second half.
"If the U.S. and Europe had cold weather at the same time, that would strain supplies a lot," Hakes said at a news conference.
In severe conditions, prices could jump an additional 7 to 8 cents, he said.

Injecting supplies of crude oil into the U.S. market from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, as suggested by Northeast lawmakers concerned about a heating oil price spike, would keep a lid on crude oil prices, but might not have much impact on heating oil supplies, EIA's markets division director said.
"U.S. refineries are running pretty close to capacity right now," said Mark Rodekohr. "You couldn't put more crude in U.S. refineries and expect to get out more heating oil."
